To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) The proportion of people who return to work within a year of their claim is relatively small, and is associated with a variety of factors, including age, marital status, and the type of condition that led to the claim.

(i) the vast majority of claimants of Incpacity Benefit are not working and are not expected by themselves to be working, (ii) the proportion of people who are not working and do not expect to work increases with age, and (iii) the proportion who are working and do not think they will be working again increases with age.

(1) the vast majority of people who claimed IB were already on the margins of the labour market; (2) the vast majority did not return to work; (3) the majority of those who did not return to paid work were employable; (4) the employability of those who did return to work increased over the course of the year; and (5) there were no significant differences between those who classified themselves as permanently unable and those who did not.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of what happens to people who claim Incapacity Benefit, a group that is often overlooked in research and policy discussions.
the question of how to identify those who can and should be expected to return to employment.
the question of who is employable among people on IB and how their employability changes over time.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ESA has been successful in identifying the majority of claimants who are likely to return to employment and in providing support and encouragement for them to do so.
the ESA is not a temporary benefit for most people, but rather a long term benefit for many people, especially those with severe health problems.
the new distinction between the Work-Related Activity Group and the Support Group has had no impact on the likelihood of people returning to work.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the majority of new IB claimants are not employable in the short term and that their employability is unlikely to improve in the medium term.

, while there is a strong association between being allocated to the Support group and not working, there are also a significant number of people in the Support Group who do not classify themselves as permanently unfit for work.

the majority of people in our sample were not employable in the year following the claim, that the majority of those who were employed at baseline were still working after one year, and that those who were employed and those who were unemployed were more likely to be in the Work-related Activity group than those who were not in employment and not seeking it.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distinction between the two groups is not a reliable guide to their employment trajectories and that the majority of claimants in the Support Group are potentially employable.
there are significant differences between people in the Support Group and those in the Work-related Activity group, and that these differences are associated with their employment trajectories.
there is a need for more nuanced policy responses to the needs of people with health-related work-limiting problems.
